## QUESTION 1

1. __Describe the quality of your classification model using 2-3 different evaluation metrics.__ You also need to explain how to define/interpret each of the evaluation metrics you use.  

I evaluated the Random Forest model that I used in Task 1 using the same six variables, settings, and s80/20 train-test split. The model was trained on 18,330 homes and evaluated on the remaining 4,583 homes. A positive prediction (1) means the home was built before 1980. It was 90% accurate, with a precision of 91.9% and a recall of 92.2%.

Accuracy: 90.03%
Accuracy is how many correct predictions are made divided by total number of predictions. It is the exact % of predictions that the model got right. This shows generally how well the model is at predicting if a home was build before or after 1980.

Precision: 91.89% 
Precision is how many homes that were correctly predicted to be before 1980 divided by the total number of homes that actually predicted to be built before 1980. This shows what % of the homes that the model predicted to be before 1980 were actually correct.

Recall: 92.18%
Recall is the number of homes correctly predicted to be built before 1980 divided by all of the actual homes that were build before 1980. This is important because of the importance of not missing homes that may contain asbestos. It shows that the model only correctly identified 92.18% of homes that may be a risk.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

homes = pl.read_csv("dwellings_ml.csv")

predictors = ["stories", "numbaths", "livearea", "basement", "quality_C", "gartype_Att"]
x = homes.select(predictors).to_numpy()
y = homes["before1980"].to_numpy()

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    x, y, test_size = 0.20, random_state = 42, stratify = y
)

model = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators = 200,
    max_depth = 15,
    min_samples_leaf = 2,
    random_state = 42,
    n_jobs = -1
)

model.fit(x_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(x_test)

# Calculate and print evaluation metrics.
accuracy = metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
precision = metrics.precision_score(y_test, predictions, pos_label = 1, zero_division = 0)
recall = metrics.recall_score(y_test, predictions, pos_label = 1, zero_division = 0)


print(f"Training homes: {len(y_train):,}; test homes: {len(y_test):,}")
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.2%}")
print(f"Precision: {precision:.2%}")
print(f"Recall: {recall:.2%}")
```


## QUESTION 2

1. __Justify your classification model by discussing the most important features selected by your model.__ This discussion should include a plot of permutation importance values for the most important features. Were there any features you thought would be importance but weren't?

The chart shows the importance of each predictor in the model. This is tested by shuffeling the values and testing to see how much the accuracy decreases when a certain value is shuffled. The more that the accuracy decreases, the more important that value is as a predictor.

Stories was the most important with a decrease of around 15%
Bathrooms was second with 11.9%
Basements was third with 11.2%
Garage was 4th with 11.1%
Quality C was 5th with 9%
Living Area was last with only around 7%

While all of the values were important, especially to reach 90% accuracy, I was suprised that living area was actually one of the least important predictors since it was one of the original 3 that I chose for my predictors in Task 1 and I had assumed that houses increasing in size was more of an indicator.

The values that I chose are justified because each affects the results by over 5% with most haveing more than 10% decrease in accuracy when shuffled.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

homes = pl.read_csv("dwellings_ml.csv")

predictors = ["stories", "numbaths", "livearea", "basement", "quality_C", "gartype_Att"]
x = homes.select(predictors).to_numpy()
y = homes["before1980"].to_numpy()

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    x, y, test_size = 0.20, random_state = 42, stratify = y
)

model = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators = 200,
    max_depth = 15,
    min_samples_leaf = 2,
    random_state = 42,
    n_jobs = -1
)

model.fit(x_train, y_train)
permutation_result = permutation_importance(
    model,
    x_test,
    y_test,
    scoring="accuracy",
    n_repeats=20,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=1
)

importance_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "feature": predictors,
    "importance_pp": permutation_result.importances_mean * 100,
    "std_pp": permutation_result.importances_std * 100
}).with_columns(
    (pl.col("importance_pp") - pl.col("std_pp")).alias("lower"),
    (pl.col("importance_pp") + pl.col("std_pp")).alias("upper")
).sort("importance_pp", descending=True)

(ggplot(importance_df.to_dict(as_series=False), aes(x="feature", y="importance_pp")) + 
    geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#2878A0") + 
    labs(
        title = "Permutation importance on the test data",
        subtitle = "Average accuracy decrease across 20 shuffles",
        x = "Predictor",
        y = "Decrease in accuracy (percentage points)"
    )
)

```

## QUESTION 3

1. __For the 3 most important features, explain their relationship to the target variable. Use a plot to illustrate the relationship.__ (3 plots minimum)

The three most important features from Question 2 were stories, bathrooms, and basement area. These three plots compare all labeled homes by construction period for each feature.

Plot 1: Stories
Homes built before 1980 typically only have 1 story with a few outliers. Meanwhile, 50% of homes build after 1980 have 1 or 2 stories with some even reaching 3 without being an outlier. This difference helps explain why stories was the most important predictor, since almost any home with more than 1 story is much less likely to have been built before 1980.

Plot 2: Bathrooms
Simmilarly to stories, homes build before 1980 had a median of 2 bathrooms with 50% of homes having 1 or 2 bathrooms. On the other hand, homes build after 1980 have a median of 3 bathrooms with 50% of homes having between 2 to 4 bathrooms. This difference helps even more to determine if a home was built before or after 1980 since if a home has 3 or more bathrooms, it is much more likely to have been built after 1980.


Plot 3: Basement area
Basement area is one that seems to have the least obvious relationship. Homes build before 1980 have a median basement size of 411 square feet with 50% of homes having between 0 to 922 square feet of basement. On the other hand, homes built after 19080 have a median basement size of 375 square feet, which is slightly less than the older homes. 50% of newer homes range from a basement of 0 to 1063 square feet. While it might be tempting to think that since the median of basement area is slightly higher for older homes, if a home has a basement, it is likely to be larger in a newer home since the 50% covers a much higher range as well as there being many high outliers for the newer homes with large basements. This means that if a house tends to have a larger basement, especially in relation to the other 2 features, it is much more likely to be a newer home.

```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn import metrics

from IPython.display import display
from pathlib import Path

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

homes = pl.read_csv("dwellings_ml.csv")

plot_data = homes.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("before1980") == 1)
        .then(pl.lit("Before 1980"))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("During or after 1980"))
        .alias("construction_period")
)

period_order = ["Before 1980", "During or after 1980"]

# Stories were the highest ranking from question 2.
plot_stories = (ggplot(
    plot_data.select(["construction_period", "stories"]).to_dict(as_series=False),
    aes(x="construction_period", y="stories")) + 
    geom_boxplot(fill="#2878A0", alpha=0.65) + 
    scale_x_discrete(limits=period_order) + 
    labs(
        title="Plot 1: Stories by construction period",
        x="Construction period", 
        y="Number of stories"
    )
)

# Bathrooms were the 2nd highest ranking from question 2.
plot_bathrooms = (ggplot(
    plot_data.select(["construction_period", "numbaths"]).to_dict(as_series=False),
    aes(x="construction_period", y="numbaths")) + 
    geom_boxplot(fill="#2878A0", alpha=0.65) + 
    scale_x_discrete(limits=period_order) + 
    labs(
        title="Plot 2: Bathrooms by construction period",
        x="Construction period", 
        y="Number of bathrooms"
    )
)

# Basement area was the 3rd highest ranking from question 2.
plot_basement = (ggplot(
    plot_data.select(["construction_period", "basement"]).to_dict(as_series=False),
    aes(x="construction_period", y="basement")) + 
    geom_boxplot(fill="#2878A0", alpha=0.65) + 
    scale_x_discrete(limits=period_order) + 
    labs(
        title="Plot 3: Basement area by construction period",
        x="Construction period", 
        y="Basement area (square feet)"
    )
)

display(plot_stories)
display(plot_bathrooms)
display(plot_basement)
```
